\title{When Debiasing Scores Reward Broken Text}

\author{Anonymous ARR submission}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Activation steering for bias is judged by a target metric that counts how often a model
produces the vocabulary marking the bias. We show that this metric can be satisfied by
destroying the response instead of debiasing it, and that the methods reporting the
strongest results are the ones this affects most. Sweeping five steering methods across
their published strength ranges on a disability-bias benchmark, 87 configurations and
21{,}750 generations, we score every response for quality alongside the target metric.
Three methods reach the metric's value for unbiased text while emitting corrupted or
repeated text, by three failure modes that no single filter on emptiness, length or
uniqueness detects. At its published setting one of them scores 201 of 250 responses as
perfectly unbiased while judged quality falls from $7.9$ to $3.2$ out of ten. Holding
quality constant reorders the comparison, and a multi-rank projection reaches comparable
debiasing at roughly half the quality cost (paired difference $+0.35$, $95\%$ CI
$[0.18, 0.53]$). We further find that the spectral statistic several recent methods use
to set an intervention's rank reports how the contrastive set was built rather than how
the bias is represented: holding the number of pairs at 13 and varying only prompt
diversity moves the top explained-variance ratio from $22\%$ to $76\%$.
\end{abstract}
